title: pool() has no deadline parameter; pooler-signed transactions that linger in the mempool execute against arbitrarily moved pool state
description: `pool(uint256 minBPT, uint256 minUSDC)` does not accept a deadline / expiry timestamp. The off-chain pooler bot computes minBPT and minUSDC from a queried/expected pool state at submission time, then signs the transaction. If the transaction is delayed (mempool congestion, gas underpricing, intentional inclusion delay by a builder), the pool's state can drift far from the quoted state by the time of inclusion — but the transaction will execute as long as the final values satisfy the original (now-stale) `minBPT`/`minUSDC` thresholds set against pre-drift expectations. Because the operator must set those thresholds permissively enough to absorb normal market movement (otherwise routine txns would revert), an attacker who can either (a) hold the tx in their bundle for several blocks or (b) wait for natural drift gets to execute pool() at a worse pool state without violating slippage. This is a standard DEX deadline pattern that Balancer's own Router contracts enforce (most Balancer Router entrypoints take a `deadline`).
exploit_path:
1. Pooler bot computes off-chain quote at block N, expects ~1.00 USDC per sUSDS (e.g., 100k sUSDS -> ~100k USDC). Sets minUSDC = 99,000 (1% tolerance), minBPT = 99,000.
2. Transaction broadcast at block N+1. Gas market is congested; the tx is not picked up by validators for 30+ blocks (6 minutes).
3. During the wait, sUSDS/waUSDC pool spot drifts to 0.995 USDC per sUSDS due to organic flow (a large minter dumped into the pool). The pool would now yield only 99,500 USDC for 100k sUSDS — still > minUSDC (99,000) so the tx executes.
4. The pooler bot would have re-quoted and either (a) cancelled or (b) widened the deposit, but had no `deadline` to force expiry.
5. Net: protocol takes a 500 USDC haircut purely from being late, with no operator opportunity to intervene.

Second exploit path — bundler / private-mempool censorship: An MEV bot or builder can hold the tx for several blocks while moving the pool with their own swaps, then release it for inclusion when the pool state is maximally adverse. Without a deadline the pooler has no way to invalidate the signed tx.
mainnet_realism: This is a generic Ethereum-mempool risk that applies to any DEX interaction. Balancer V3's own Router contracts include `deadline` as a standard parameter on swap/add/remove entrypoints. The yield-claim-nft V2 contracts route through the Vault unlock() pattern directly and skip the Router's deadline check. With current builder-market dynamics and private-mempool RPCs (Flashbots, Eden, Bloxroute) it is realistic for a tx to be deliberately held for several blocks (or rejected and re-broadcast). The realised cost depends on volatility of sUSDS/waUSDC over the delay window; in normal conditions a few basis points per minute is typical for stable pools.
recommendation: Add `uint256 deadline` to pool() and require(block.timestamp <= deadline, ...). Match the convention used by Balancer's own Router (which takes deadline as the last argument). Update the pooler bot to set deadline = block.timestamp + 30 seconds or similar.
severity_rationale: Downgraded from initial Medium guess to Low/QA. Missing-deadline is a well-known DEX best-practice issue. In this contract, minBPT/minUSDC still provide first-order slippage protection — the harm from a delayed tx only materialises if (a) the operator-set thresholds were loose enough to absorb significant pool drift AND (b) the tx is delayed long enough for that drift to materialise. The function is also onlyAuthorizedPooler, so the operator (not an external attacker) is the entity bearing the risk and has tools (private mempool, gas pricing) to manage it. This is a spec-deviation / hardening recommendation rather than a value leak with realistic attack path. Per C4: 'State handling, function incorrect as to spec, issues with comments' — fits QA/Low. Combined with ECON-RAW-001/002 as part of the broader 'pool() lacks defensive parameters' theme.
